title: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
summary: Contribute to a project you cannot push to: fork and add an upstream remote, rebase onto current upstream, fold review fixes in with --fixup, force-push safely, sign off per the DCO.
outcomes: Set up origin and upstream remotes and explain why upstream/main is only as fresh as your last fetch
Predict which commits get new hashes when you rebase onto upstream or autosquash a fixup
Use git commit --fixup and git rebase -i --autosquash to fold a review fix into the right commit
Explain when --force-with-lease protects a maintainer's commit and why --force-if-includes is needed too
Explain what a Signed-off-by trailer certifies under the DCO and how each GitHub merge method lands commits

lessons.title: Fork, clone and two remotes: origin and upstream

blocks.md:
You want to fix a bug in a project you cannot push to. GitHub's answer is a **fork**: a server-side copy of the repository under your account. You push to your fork, then open a **pull request** (PR) asking the original project to pull a branch from your fork into one of its branches.

The original project is called the **upstream** repository. In a PR from a fork, the **base branch** is the upstream branch you want to merge into, and the **compare** (head) branch is the branch in your fork that holds your changes.

A **remote** is a short name your local clone uses for another repository's URL. After `git clone` of your fork, the only remote is `origin`, pointing at your fork. GitHub's fork guide then has you add a second remote named `upstream` pointing at the original repository. From then on you **fetch** from upstream (to see the project's new work) and **push** to origin (your fork).

blocks.title: Three repositories, two remotes, one pull request

nodes.label:
pull request
base: main  compare: fix-parser

scenes.caption: You start with only the upstream repository, which you can read but not push to.
Forking makes a copy on GitHub under your account. It is a separate repository that you control.
Cloning your fork gives you a local repository whose one remote, `origin`, is your fork.
`git remote add upstream URL` records the original repository too. Now `git fetch upstream` brings its new commits into your clone, read-only.
Your work travels one way: commit locally, push to origin. You never push to upstream; you lack permission, and it is not how the project accepts changes.
The PR joins the two: it asks upstream to merge your fork's branch into its base branch. Maintainers review it there.

blocks.code:
git clone https://github.com/YOU/repo.git
cd repo
git remote add upstream https://github.com/ORIGINAL-OWNER/repo.git
git remote -v
# origin    https://github.com/YOU/repo.git (fetch)
# origin    https://github.com/YOU/repo.git (push)
# upstream  https://github.com/ORIGINAL-OWNER/repo.git (fetch)
# upstream  https://github.com/ORIGINAL-OWNER/repo.git (push)
git fetch upstream
git switch -c fix-parser upstream/main
blocks.caption: The setup from GitHub's fork guide, then a topic branch started from the newest upstream commit. `gh repo fork REPO --clone=true` does the fork, clone and upstream remote in one step.

blocks.md: `git fetch upstream` stores what it downloads in **remote-tracking branches** such as `upstream/main`. These are local, read-only bookmarks recording where upstream's branches were *the last time you fetched*. Nothing updates them in the background: if the project merges ten PRs this afternoon, your `upstream/main` stays where it was until you fetch again.

blocks.title: Remote-tracking refs move only when you fetch

scenes.caption: Simulated with real git: upstream has 3 commits. You fetched, branched from `upstream/main` and made commits A and B.
A maintainer merges two commits upstream. The server moves on, but your `upstream/main` still says U3: your clone has not asked.
`git fetch upstream` copies U4 and U5 down and moves `upstream/main`. Your branch is untouched: fetch never changes your own branches.

blocks.prompt: Right after the maintainer's two new commits land, but before you fetch, you run `git rev-list --left-right --count upstream/main...HEAD` (it prints commits only on the left side, then only on the right). What does it print?
blocks.reveal:
It prints `0  2`: zero commits behind, two ahead. Git compares against your local `upstream/main`, which still points at U3. After `git fetch upstream` the same command prints `2  2` (two behind, two ahead). Both outputs come from running this exact scenario in a scratch repository.

The lesson: any "am I up to date?" check is only as fresh as your last fetch.

blocks.md: Misconception: "syncing my fork" updates my laptop. GitHub's Sync fork button updates the fork on GitHub; `git fetch upstream` plus a merge updates your local copy. GitHub's docs point out that syncing locally does not update the fork on GitHub until you push. They are separate repositories.
Fetch from `upstream`, push to `origin`. Remote-tracking branches like `upstream/main` are snapshots from your last fetch, not live views.

blocks.question: You cloned your fork and ran `git fetch upstream`, but it fails with "'upstream' does not appear to be a git repository". What is the most likely cause?
options: Your fork is out of date with the original repository
You never ran `git remote add upstream URL`, so the name is unknown
You need to push to origin before you can fetch
The original repository has a different default branch name
blocks.explain: Cloning creates only the `origin` remote. `upstream` is just a name you add yourself with `git remote add`; until then Git does not know what it refers to. Being out of date or having a different default branch does not make the remote name unknown.

blocks.question: You open a PR from YOU/repo branch `fix-parser` into ORIGINAL-OWNER/repo `main`. Which is the base branch?
options: `fix-parser` in your fork
`main` in your fork
`main` in the upstream repository
`upstream/main` in your local clone
blocks.explain: The base branch is where the changes would be merged: the upstream repository's `main`. The compare (head) branch is `fix-parser` in your fork. `upstream/main` is only your local bookmark and does not exist on GitHub.

lessons.title: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main

blocks.md: While your PR waits, upstream keeps moving. Maintainers usually want your branch to sit on top of the current base branch, so the diff shows only your change and CI tests it against today's code. You have two ways to catch up: **merge** upstream into your branch, which adds a merge commit, or **rebase** your branch onto upstream, which rewrites your commits so they start from the new tip.

The git-rebase manual describes `git rebase <upstream>` in four steps:

1. List the commits on your branch since it branched off `<upstream>` that have no equivalent commit already in `<upstream>`.
2. Check out `<upstream>` (detached).
3. Replay the listed commits one by one, like `git cherry-pick`.
4. Point your branch at the last replayed commit.

The branch-off point is the **merge base**: the newest commit both histories share.

blocks.title: git rebase upstream/main, with real hashes

scenes.caption: After `git fetch upstream`: upstream gained U4 and U5. Your two commits, 820db75 and a28201a, still sit on U3, the merge base.
Step 1: list your commits not in upstream/main: 820db75 then a28201a. Step 2: start from upstream's tip, U5.
Step 3: replay 820db75 on U5. Same change, new parent, so a new commit: cf67b63. A commit's hash covers its parent, so it cannot keep the old hash.
Replay a28201a too, giving a7b91cf. Step 4 moves `fix-parser` there. The old commits are no longer on any branch, though the reflog still remembers them.

blocks.md: All hashes here come from running the workflow in a scratch repository with fixed dates, so they are reproducible. The figure shortens them to 6 characters to fit.

blocks.title: Commits behind and ahead of upstream/main

scenes.caption: Before fetching: `0 behind, 2 ahead`. Looks current, but the reference is stale.
After `git fetch upstream`: `2 behind, 2 ahead`. The branches have diverged.
After `git rebase upstream/main`: `0 behind, 2 ahead`. Same two changes, now on top of U5.

blocks.code:
git fetch upstream
git rebase upstream/main
# on a conflict, rebase stops at that commit:
git status                 # shows the conflicted files
# edit the files, then
git add parser.c
git rebase --continue
# or give up and restore the branch as it was:
git rebase --abort
blocks.caption: The conflict commands are the three the git-rebase manual lists: resolve and --continue, --abort, or --skip the commit.

blocks.prompt: Why not just merge `upstream/main` into `fix-parser` instead? Think about what the PR's commit list would show after a few rounds of catching up.
blocks.reveal: Each catch-up adds a merge commit to your branch, so the PR fills with "Merge branch 'main' into fix-parser" commits that are not part of your change. Many projects ask contributors to rebase instead so the branch is just their commits on top of the current base. Merging is not wrong; some projects prefer it because it never rewrites published commits. Read the project's CONTRIBUTING file.

blocks.md: Rebase rewrites history. Pro Git's rule: do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on. Your own PR branch is the usual exception, which is why the next lesson's force-push needs care, not a ban.
Rebasing replays your commits on a new base. Every replayed commit gets a new hash because its parent changed, even if its diff is identical.

blocks.question: You rebase a 3-commit branch onto a newer `upstream/main`. No conflicts occur, and the diffs are byte-for-byte the same. How many of your 3 commits keep their original hashes?
options: All 3, because the content did not change
Only the first, because it is closest to the base
None, because each commit's parent changed
It depends on whether you used --autosquash
blocks.explain: A commit's hash covers its tree, its parent hash, its author, committer and message. Replaying onto a new base gives the first commit a new parent, which gives it a new hash, which then changes the parent of the second commit, and so on up the chain.

blocks.question: Halfway through a rebase, Git stops with a conflict in `parser.c` and you are unsure of your fix. Which command returns the branch to exactly where it was before you started?
options: `git rebase --skip`
`git rebase --abort`
`git rebase --continue`
`git reset --hard upstream/main`
blocks.explain: `--abort` stops the rebase and restores the original branch. `--skip` drops the conflicting commit and keeps going, which loses that change. `--continue` needs the conflict resolved and staged. Resetting to upstream/main throws away all your commits.

lessons.title: Folding review fixes into the right commit with --fixup

blocks.md: A reviewer comments: "`handle empty input` crashes on a null pointer." You fix it. If you add a commit called "fix review comment", the history now contains a known-broken commit followed by its repair. Projects that review commit by commit, or bisect later, want each commit to be correct on its own, so they ask you to put the fix *into* the commit it belongs to.

Git has a built-in tool for this. `git commit --fixup=<commit>` makes a new commit whose title is `fixup! ` followed by the target commit's title. Later, `git rebase -i --autosquash` finds each such commit, moves it right after its target, and changes its action from `pick` to `fixup`, which melds its changes into the target and throws away its message. The target keeps its own message and authorship.

blocks.title: What autosquash does to the todo list
blocks.code:
git commit --fixup=cf67b63
git rebase -i --autosquash upstream/main

# todo list as written (top runs first):
pick cf67b63 parser: handle empty input
fixup 732b939 fixup! parser: handle empty input
pick a7b91cf parser: add tests
pick 7a7788e parser: test unicode input

# result: git log --format='%h %s' upstream/main..HEAD
7af2db7 parser: test unicode input
9782e95 parser: add tests
e7b122d parser: handle empty input

scenes.caption: You commit the null-pointer fix with `--fixup` pointing at the commit it repairs. Git writes the title for you.
Meanwhile you also add an unrelated new commit, 7a7788e. Now run the interactive rebase with autosquash.
Git builds the todo list. It matched the `fixup!` title to cf67b63, moved 732b939 directly below it and set its action to `fixup`.
The other commits stay `pick`. Note they still get replayed: 7a7788e was after the fixup, and a7b91cf now sits on a rewritten parent.
Result: 3 commits. The fix is inside e7b122d. Every commit from the edited one upward has a new hash; the base U5 is untouched.
scenes.output:
7af2db7 parser: test unicode input
9782e95 parser: add tests
e7b122d parser: handle empty input

blocks.md: The commit message of `e7b122d` is unchanged: its subject, then a blank line, then `Signed-off-by: Ada Dev <ada@example.org>`. The fixup commit's own message was discarded, just as the git-commit manual says.

Related variants from the git-commit manual:

- `--fixup=amend:<commit>` makes an `amend!` commit, which changes the content *and* replaces the target's message.
- `--fixup=reword:<commit>` replaces only the message, ignoring staged changes.
- `--squash=<commit>` makes a `squash!` commit; autosquash marks it `squash`, which keeps both messages for you to edit.

Setting `rebase.autoSquash=true` makes interactive rebases autosquash by default.

blocks.prompt: You rebase with `--autosquash` but forget `-i`. Does the squashing still happen?
blocks.reveal: It depends on your Git version. The Git 2.44 release notes say `--autosquash` is now enabled for non-interactive rebase. On older Git, such as the 2.39 used for this course's examples, it only acts with `-i`: in our scratch repository the `fixup!` commit was left unsquashed. Writing `-i --autosquash` works on both, and lets you review the list first.

blocks.md: Fixup commits are not magic on their own. If you push `fixup!` commits and never autosquash, a merge-commit or rebase-and-merge PR lands them on main exactly as they are, `fixup!` titles and all. Autosquash before asking for the final merge unless the project says otherwise.
`git commit --fixup=X` then `git rebase -i --autosquash BASE` puts a fix into commit X without editing the todo list by hand. Every commit after X gets a new hash.

blocks.question: Your branch has commits P (parser), T (tests), then a `fixup! parser` commit F. After `git rebase -i --autosquash upstream/main`, what does the todo list contain?
options: pick P, pick T, fixup F
pick P, pick T, squash F
fixup F, pick P, pick T
pick P, fixup F, pick T
blocks.explain: Autosquash moves each `fixup!` commit directly after the commit whose title it names and turns its `pick` into `fixup`. So F lands between P and T. `squash` is used only for `squash!` commits, and a fixup never runs before its target.

blocks.question: You want to fix a typo in the *message* of an earlier commit without changing any code, and let autosquash apply it. Which command creates the right commit?
options: `git commit --fixup=<commit>`
`git commit --squash=<commit>`
`git commit --fixup=reword:<commit>`
`git commit --amend`
blocks.explain: `--fixup=reword:` creates an `amend!` commit that replaces the target's message and ignores staged changes. Plain `--fixup` keeps the target's message. `--amend` only rewrites the latest commit, not an earlier one.

lessons.title: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits

blocks.md: After a rebase, your local `fix-parser` and the one on your fork have **diverged**: the fork has a7b91cf, you have 7af2db7, and neither contains the other. A plain `git push` refuses because it would not be a **fast-forward** (the remote tip is not an ancestor of what you push). You must force. The question is how to force without destroying work you have not seen.

Someone else *can* push to your PR branch. When you open a PR from a user-owned fork, GitHub offers **Allow edits from maintainers**, which lets people with push access to upstream push commits to your branch, for example to fix a typo before merging. If a maintainer did that while you were rebasing, `git push --force` would silently delete their commit.

blocks.title: Force pushing after a maintainer touched your branch

scenes.caption: You pushed your rebased branch earlier; your remote-tracking ref `origin/fix-parser` records a7b91cf.
The maintainer pushes a docs commit on top. The fork's tip is now c1d0e50. Meanwhile you autosquashed locally to 7af2db7.
Plain push: rejected `(fetch first)`. The fork holds c1d0e50, a commit your clone has never seen, so Git refuses to overwrite it. Git is protecting the remote.
`--force-with-lease`: Git expects the remote to still be at your tracking value a7b91cf. It is at c1d0e50, so the push is rejected `(stale info)`. The maintainer's commit survives.

Trap: you run `git fetch origin` (or your editor does it for you). Now `origin/fix-parser` is c1d0e50, the lease matches, and a dry run shows the push would succeed as a forced update, deleting c1d0e50.
Adding `--force-if-includes` checks that the fetched tip c1d0e50 is reachable from your branch's reflog. It never was, so Git rejects `(remote ref updated since checkout)`.

blocks.md:
Every rejection message above is the real output of Git 2.39 in a scratch repository. The rules come straight from the git-push manual:

- `--force-with-lease` alone protects each ref being updated by requiring its current remote value to equal your remote-tracking branch for it.
- `--force-with-lease=<ref>:<expect>` compares against a value you name explicitly instead.
- `--force-if-includes`, used with a lease that has no explicit value, also requires the remote-tracking tip to be reachable from your local branch's reflog, meaning you actually integrated it.

blocks.code:
git fetch origin
git log --oneline HEAD..origin/fix-parser    # anything here is not in your branch
# c1d0e50 docs: note from maintainer
git cherry-pick c1d0e50                      # bring it in as a copy
git push --force-with-lease=fix-parser:c1d0e50 origin fix-parser
blocks.caption: Safe recovery: inspect what the remote has, integrate it, then force with a lease naming the exact tip you inspected. A cherry-pick copies c1d0e50, so `--force-if-includes` still rejects; the explicit lease is the guard.

blocks.md: The manual's own warning: a bare `--force-with-lease` interacts very badly with anything that runs `git fetch` in the background, such as an IDE or a cron job. Each background fetch refreshes the expectation, so the lease can no longer tell "I saw this" from "something fetched this".
Plain `--force` disables the fast-forward check and the lease checks and can make the remote lose commits. There is rarely a reason to use it on a shared PR branch.
`--force-with-lease` says "overwrite only if the remote is still what I last fetched". Add `--force-if-includes` so a fetch alone does not count as having seen the remote's commits.

blocks.question: You rebase, your IDE silently runs `git fetch` every few minutes, and a maintainer pushed to your PR branch an hour ago. You run `git push --force-with-lease`. What happens?
options: It is rejected with stale info, because the maintainer's commit is newer than your rebase
It succeeds and overwrites the maintainer's commit, because the background fetch already updated your remote-tracking ref
It succeeds and keeps both, because a lease merges the histories
It is rejected because leases cannot be used on forks
blocks.explain: A bare lease compares the remote with your remote-tracking ref. The background fetch moved that ref to the maintainer's commit, so the lease matches and the forced update goes through. `--force-if-includes` would catch this, because the commit never appeared in your branch's reflog.

blocks.question: Why does a plain `git push` fail right after a successful `git rebase upstream/main` on a branch you had already pushed?
options: The pushed commits were rewritten, so the remote tip is no longer an ancestor of your local tip
Rebase deletes the remote branch
GitHub blocks pushes to branches that have an open PR
Rebase changes the remote URL of origin
blocks.explain: Without force, git push only accepts fast-forward updates. Rebasing replaced your commits with new ones, so the old remote tip is no longer in your branch's history. Pushing to a branch with an open PR is normal and updates the PR.

lessons.title: Sign-off, the DCO, and how your commits land upstream

blocks.md: Many projects (the Linux kernel and Git itself among them) require every commit to carry a line like `Signed-off-by: Ada Dev <ada@example.org>`. This is a **trailer**: a `Key: value` line in the final paragraph of a commit message. `git commit -s` (long form `--signoff`) adds it using your configured committer name and email.

The git-commit manual is careful about what it means: the meaning of a sign-off depends on the project. For the kernel and Git, it certifies the **Developer Certificate of Origin** (DCO) 1.1, a short statement published by the Linux Foundation. By signing off you certify one of three things:

- (a) you created it, in whole or in part, and have the right to submit it under the open source license indicated in the file, or
- (b) it is based on earlier work under a suitable open source license that lets you submit it, or
- (c) someone who certified (a), (b) or (c) gave it to you and you did not change it.

And (d) you understand the contribution and your sign-off, including personal information, are public and kept indefinitely.

blocks.title: Anatomy of a signed-off commit message

scenes.caption: Line 0 is the subject, `parser: handle empty input`. A blank line separates it from the body.
The body explains why. Trailers go in the last paragraph, after another blank line.
`git commit -s` appends `Signed-off-by: Ada Dev <ada@example.org>`. It certifies the DCO; it is not a cryptographic signature.
Simplified: if a patch passes through another maintainer, the kernel docs describe them adding their own sign-off below, building a chain of who handled it.

blocks.code:
git commit -s -m "parser: handle empty input"

# forgot -s on existing commits? add it to every commit being rebased:
git rebase --signoff upstream/main
git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes origin fix-parser

# check:
git log --format='%h %(trailers:key=Signed-off-by)' upstream/main..HEAD
blocks.caption: `git rebase --signoff` adds the trailer to all rebased commits (with -i, only to commits that are picked, edited or reworded). Git has no config option to sign off by default; the git-commit manual points to gitfaq for why.

blocks.md: Misconception: `-s` signs the commit. It does not. `-s` (lowercase) adds a Signed-off-by text trailer, a legal statement. `-S` (uppercase, `--gpg-sign`) adds a cryptographic signature that GitHub can show as Verified. A project may require either, both, or neither.

Once approved, a maintainer merges your PR with one of GitHub's three methods. What lands on the base branch differs:

- **Create a merge commit** (the default): all your commits plus one merge commit, made with `--no-ff`.
- **Squash and merge**: your commits are combined into one commit. You lose per-commit history, and if you keep working on the same branch and open a new PR, already-squashed commits show up again.
- **Rebase and merge**: each commit is added individually with no merge commit. GitHub always creates new SHAs and updates the committer, and drops originally empty commits.

blocks.title: Commits added to main for our 3-commit PR

scenes.caption: Merge commit: your 3 commits plus 1 merge commit, so 4 new commits on main, with your original hashes preserved.
Squash: 1 commit. Your careful split into parser, tests and unicode tests disappears from main's history.
Rebase and merge: 3 commits, linear history, but with new hashes, so `git log` on main will not show 7af2db7.

blocks.md: Because squash and rebase-and-merge create new commits, `git branch -d fix-parser` may say the branch is not fully merged after your PR lands. Check the PR page, then delete with `-D` if you are sure.
`-s` adds a Signed-off-by trailer whose meaning the project defines (often the DCO). Read CONTRIBUTING to learn whether the project wants sign-offs, fixups squashed, and which merge method it uses.

blocks.question: A project's CI says "DCO check failed: commit 9782e95 has no Signed-off-by". The other two commits are signed off. What is the cleanest fix?
options: Add a comment on the PR saying you agree to the DCO
Run `git commit -S` to sign the latest commit with GPG
Run `git rebase --signoff upstream/main`, then force-push with a lease
Close the PR and open a new one with a different branch name
blocks.explain: The trailer must be in the commit message itself, so the commit has to be rewritten. `git rebase --signoff` adds it to every replayed commit (in our test, commits that already ended with the same trailer did not get a second copy), then you update the PR with a guarded force-push. `-S` is a cryptographic signature, not a sign-off.

blocks.question: Your 3-commit PR is merged with "Rebase and merge". Back in your clone, `git fetch upstream` then `git log upstream/main` does not show 7af2db7. Why?
options: GitHub dropped your commits because they were signed off
Rebase and merge recreates each commit with new SHAs and updated committer information
Your fetch is stale and needs to be repeated
Rebase and merge always squashes into one commit
blocks.explain: GitHub's docs say Rebase and merge always updates the committer information and creates new commit SHAs. Your changes are there, but as new commits with the same content and messages. Squashing is a different merge method.
